faq.title: Frequently asked questions about online diet and online dietitian
faq.subtitle: Questions about online diet, nutrition plan or dietitian subscription? We have the answers.
faq.metaTitle: FAQ – Online diet and online dietitian
faq.metaDescription: Frequently asked questions about online diet, AI dietitian, dietitian subscription and online nutrition plan. Find out how the platform works.
faq.noResults: No questions found matching your search.
faq.cat1q1: How does an online diet with AI and a dietitian work?
faq.cat1a1: Our platform combines AI technology with the expertise of a certified dietitian. The AI dietitian analyzes your dietary assessment, goals and health status, then creates a personalized online nutrition plan. In paid plans, a dietitian verifies the recommendations and approves the final version.
faq.cat1q2: How long does it take to prepare an online nutrition plan?
faq.cat1a2: The assessment takes about 3–5 minutes. The nutrition plan is created by AI and submitted to the dietitian for approval. The final version appears in your user dashboard within 24 hours of approval.
faq.cat1q3: Is the online diet tailored to my goal (weight loss, muscle gain, health)?
faq.cat1a3: Yes. The online nutrition plan is created individually based on your goal, lifestyle, allergies and food preferences.
faq.cat1q4: Can I use multiple online diets at the same time (e.g. for a couple)?
faq.cat1a4: Currently, one online nutrition plan is assigned to one person. We are working on an option for couples and families.
faq.cat2q1: What does an online nutrition plan include?
faq.cat2a1: Every online nutrition plan includes: exact product weights, household measures (tablespoon, cup, piece), macronutrients and calories, shopping list, meal preparation instructions and the option to swap meals (in paid plans).
faq.cat2q2: Can I swap meals in my online diet?
faq.cat2a2: Yes. In paid plans you can choose from several alternatives for each meal, keeping calorie consistency.
faq.cat2q3: Does the online diet account for allergies and intolerances?
faq.cat2a3: Yes. During the assessment you indicate allergies and intolerances, which the AI dietitian takes into account when creating the plan.
faq.cat2q4: Is a Thermomix or Air fryer version available?
faq.cat2a4: Yes. When purchasing an online nutrition plan, you can select an additional Thermomix or Air fryer option.
faq.cat2q5: Does the online diet work on mobile?
faq.cat2a5: Yes. The user dashboard is fully responsive on phones and tablets. No app installation required.
faq.cat3q1: Does the dietitian subscription renew automatically?
faq.cat3a1: Yes. The dietitian subscription in the monthly plan renews automatically each month. The one-time plan does not renew automatically.
faq.cat3q2: What is the difference between a one-time plan and a dietitian subscription?
faq.cat3a2: A one-time plan is an online diet without auto-renewal. A dietitian subscription provides continuous care and regular updates without the need to repurchase.
faq.cat3q3: Can I cancel my dietitian subscription?
faq.cat3a3: Yes. You can cancel your dietitian subscription at any time in your user dashboard.
faq.cat3q4: Do I have 14 days to withdraw from the agreement?
faq.cat3a4: Yes. Under consumer law, you may withdraw from an online contract within 14 days.
faq.cat4q1: How is data protected in an online diet?
faq.cat4a1: Data is processed in accordance with GDPR. We use AES-256 encryption and restricted administrative access. We never sell your data.
faq.cat4q2: Does an online diet replace a doctor's visit?
faq.cat4a2: No. An online diet and an AI dietitian do not replace medical consultation. In case of chronic diseases, we recommend consulting your physician.

howAiWorks.title: How AI diet planning works
howAiWorks.subtitle: Discover our unique process combining artificial intelligence with the expertise of a clinical dietitian. Every plan is created individually and verified by a specialist.
howAiWorks.metaTitle: How AI diet planning works — e-dietetyk.com
howAiWorks.metaDescription: Learn how AI creates personalized nutrition plans: assessment, AI analysis, 85 clinical rules, OR-Tools optimization, dietitian review. Safe and GDPR-compliant.
howAiWorks.processSubtitle: From dietary assessment to finished plan — the entire process takes less than 24 hours.
howAiWorks.step1Title: You fill out the dietary assessment
howAiWorks.step1Desc: A short questionnaire (3–5 minutes) about your goals, preferences, allergies, health status and lifestyle.
howAiWorks.step2Desc: The algorithm calculates your energy needs (BMR, TDEE), target macronutrients and nutrition goals based on scientific data.
howAiWorks.step3Desc: 85 clinical rules and 16 safety checks (red flags) evaluate the plan against your health conditions. Critical cases are routed to manual review.
howAiWorks.step4Desc: A mathematical solver (Google OR-Tools CP-SAT) selects optimal meals from 6,600+ Polish food products — balancing calories, macros, micros, diversity and seasonality.
howAiWorks.step5Desc: A licensed clinical dietitian reviews the plan, verifies clinical safety and nutritional adequacy, and makes adjustments if needed.
howAiWorks.step6Title: You receive your plan + shopping list
howAiWorks.step6Desc: The approved plan appears in your dashboard — with recipes, exact weights, a categorized shopping list and the option to swap meals.
howAiWorks.safetySubtitle: Your health is our priority. Every plan goes through multi-level checks.
howAiWorks.safety1: 85 clinical rules covering diabetes, hypertension, celiac disease, pregnancy and more
howAiWorks.safety2: 16 safety checks (red flags) with automatic escalation to a dietitian
howAiWorks.safety3: AES-256-GCM encryption for all medical data
howAiWorks.safety4: Full GDPR compliance — we never sell your data
howAiWorks.safety5: Mandatory review of every plan by a licensed dietitian
howAiWorks.comparisonSubtitle: We combine the speed of AI with the expertise of a clinical dietitian.

glossary.title: Nutrition Glossary
glossary.subtitle: Learn the key terms in dietetics, nutrition and health. Every definition prepared by e-dietetyk.com specialists.
glossary.metaTitle: Nutrition Glossary — dietary terms from A to Z
glossary.metaDescription: Comprehensive nutrition glossary: BMI, BMR, macronutrients, glycemic index, diets and health conditions. Definitions by licensed dietitians.
glossary.noResults: No term found matching your search.
glossary.ctaTitle: Ready to put this knowledge into practice?
glossary.ctaSubtitle: Order a personalized AI-powered nutrition plan based on science.
glossary.t1def: A ratio of body weight (kg) to height squared (m). Used for initial assessment of whether body weight is within a healthy range. Values: <18.5 underweight, 18.5–24.9 normal, 25–29.9 overweight, ≥30 obese. Does not account for body composition (muscle vs fat mass).
glossary.t2def: The minimum amount of energy (kcal) the body needs at rest to maintain vital functions — breathing, circulation, thermoregulation. Calculated based on sex, age, body weight and height (e.g. Harris-Benedict or Mifflin-St Jeor equation).
glossary.t3def: Total daily energy requirement, calculated as BMR multiplied by the physical activity level (PAL). Accounts for daily activities, exercise and the thermic effect of food. The basis for setting diet calorie targets.
glossary.t4def: The difference between energy consumed from food and energy expended by the body. A positive balance (surplus) leads to weight gain, a negative balance (deficit) to weight loss. A zero balance maintains current weight.
glossary.t5def: A state where you consume fewer calories than your TDEE. A safe deficit is typically 300–500 kcal/day, allowing loss of 0.5–1 kg per week. An excessive deficit can lead to muscle loss and metabolic slowdown.
glossary.t6def: A state where you consume more calories than your TDEE. A controlled surplus (200–400 kcal/day) is used for muscle building. An uncontrolled surplus leads to fat tissue gain.
glossary.t7def: A way of eating — the overall pattern of food products and eating habits. In a clinical context: a planned menu tailored to individual health needs, goals and preferences. Diet is not only about weight loss — it also includes therapeutic, sports and preventive diets.
glossary.t8def: A detailed menu for a set period (e.g. a week, a month) containing specific meals, recipes, product weights and nutritional values. At e-dietetyk.com, plans are generated by AI and verified by a clinical dietitian.
glossary.t9def: A building macronutrient — made of amino acids, essential for building and repairing muscles, producing enzymes and hormones, and immune function. Daily requirement: 0.8–2.0 g/kg body weight (depending on activity). Sources: meat, fish, eggs, dairy, legumes, tofu.
glossary.t10def: Easily absorbed sugars — glucose, fructose, sucrose. They raise blood glucose levels quickly (high glycemic index). Sources: sugar, honey, sweets, white bread, fruits. Should make up no more than 10% of daily energy.
glossary.t11def: Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen) — digested more slowly, providing stable energy. They have a lower glycemic index than simple sugars. Sources: groats, wholegrain bread, brown rice, potatoes, legumes.
glossary.t12def: Fatty acids with no double bonds in the carbon chain. Excess raises LDL cholesterol levels and increases cardiovascular disease risk. Sources: butter, lard, fatty meats, palm oil, coconut oil. Recommended intake: <10% of daily energy.
glossary.t13def: Fatty acids with one (monounsaturated, MUFA) or multiple (polyunsaturated, PUFA) double bonds. Beneficial for the cardiovascular system. Sources: olive oil, avocado, nuts, oily fish. Includes omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids.
glossary.t14def: An indigestible fraction of carbohydrates — regulates bowel movements, supports gut microbiota, lowers cholesterol and stabilizes blood sugar. Daily requirement: 25–40 g. Sources: vegetables, fruits, whole grains, seeds, legumes.
glossary.t15def: Amino acids the body cannot produce on its own — they must come from the diet. There are 9: leucine, isoleucine, valine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan, histidine. Complete sources: meat, eggs, dairy, soy, quinoa.
glossary.t16def: Polyunsaturated fatty acids (EPA, DHA, ALA) with anti-inflammatory effects. Support brain, heart and nervous system function. Sources: oily fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines), flaxseed, walnuts, rapeseed oil. Recommended: 250–500 mg EPA+DHA daily.
glossary.t17def: A micronutrient essential for oxygen transport (haemoglobin) and energy production. Deficiency leads to anaemia. Haem iron (meat, fish) is better absorbed than non-haem iron (legumes, spinach). Vitamin C enhances iron absorption.
glossary.t18def: The main building material for bones and teeth, essential for muscle contractions, blood clotting and nerve conduction. Daily requirement: 1000–1200 mg. Sources: dairy, sardines, calcium-set tofu, broccoli, mineral water. Absorption requires vitamin D.
glossary.t19def: A fat-soluble vitamin crucial for calcium absorption, bone health, immunity and muscle function. Synthesized in the skin under UV-B radiation. Supplementation widely recommended (800–2000 IU/day). Dietary sources: oily fish, eggs, mushrooms.
glossary.t20def: Essential for DNA synthesis, cell division and proper fetal development. Critical in pregnancy — deficiency increases neural tube defect risk. Recommended intake: 400 µg/day (600 µg in pregnancy). Sources: dark leafy greens, legumes, liver.
glossary.t21def: Essential for red blood cell formation, nervous system function and DNA synthesis. Found exclusively in animal products — vegetarians and vegans must supplement. Deficiency leads to megaloblastic anaemia and neuropathy. Sources: meat, fish, eggs, dairy.
glossary.t22def: A micronutrient involved in over 300 enzymatic reactions. Supports immunity, wound healing, taste and smell, and protein synthesis. Daily requirement: 8–11 mg. Sources: red meat, seafood (oysters), pumpkin seeds, nuts, whole grains.
glossary.t23def: Involved in over 600 metabolic processes — blood pressure regulation, muscle and nerve function, protein synthesis, glucose metabolism. Deficiency manifests as muscle cramps, fatigue, irritability. Sources: nuts, seeds, dark chocolate, spinach, avocado.
glossary.t24def: An electrolyte regulating blood pressure, fluid-electrolyte balance and muscle function (including the heart). A potassium-rich diet reduces hypertension risk. Daily requirement: 3500–4700 mg. Sources: bananas, potatoes, tomatoes, avocado, legumes.
glossary.t25def: An electrolyte essential for osmotic pressure regulation and neuromuscular function. Excess (>2000 mg/day) increases hypertension risk. Main source: table salt and processed foods. WHO recommends limiting intake to 5 g of salt/day.
glossary.t26def: A potent antioxidant, essential for collagen synthesis, non-haem iron absorption and immune function. The body cannot synthesize it. Daily requirement: 75–90 mg. Sources: bell peppers, citrus fruits, kiwi, blackcurrant, broccoli.
glossary.t27def: A classification of foods by their effect on blood glucose levels after consumption, on a scale of 0–100 (glucose = 100). Low GI (<55): groats, legumes. Medium (56–69): basmati rice, rye bread. High (>70): white bread, potatoes, sweets. A key parameter in diabetic diets.
glossary.t28def: Takes into account both the glycemic index and the amount of carbohydrates in a serving. Better reflects the actual impact of a meal on blood sugar than GI alone. Formula: GL = (GI × g carbs in serving) / 100. Low GL: <10, medium: 11–19, high: ≥20.
glossary.t29def: Measures the body's insulin response to consuming a given food, independent of the glycemic index. Some foods (e.g. dairy, whey protein) trigger a strong insulin response despite a low GI. Important for managing insulin resistance.
glossary.t30def: The ratio of waist circumference to hip circumference — an indicator of fat distribution. Abdominal obesity (WHR >0.9 in men, >0.85 in women) is associated with increased risk of metabolic disease, type 2 diabetes and cardiovascular disease.
glossary.t31def: A condition where the body's cells respond poorly to insulin, leading to elevated blood glucose and insulin levels. A risk factor for type 2 diabetes, PCOS and fatty liver disease. Dietary treatment: low-glycemic diet, regular meals, fibre, physical activity.
glossary.t32def: An autoimmune disease where consuming gluten (a protein in wheat, rye, barley) damages intestinal villi and impairs nutrient absorption. The only treatment: a strict lifelong gluten-free diet. Diagnosis: antibody testing + intestinal biopsy.
glossary.t33def: Excessive bacterial growth in the small intestine, causing bloating, abdominal pain, diarrhoea and malabsorption. Treatment includes antibiotics and a low-FODMAP diet. Diagnosis: hydrogen-methane breath test.
glossary.t34def: A diagnostic and therapeutic strategy involving temporary exclusion of suspected foods (e.g. dairy, gluten, eggs) from the menu, followed by gradual reintroduction to identify a food allergen or intolerance.
glossary.t35def: A high-fat, low-carbohydrate diet (<50 g carbs/day) that forces ketosis — a metabolic state where the body uses ketone bodies as its main energy source instead of glucose. Used for epilepsy, weight loss and insulin resistance. Requires specialist supervision.
glossary.t36def: A dietary pattern based on traditional cuisine of Mediterranean countries. Rich in vegetables, fruits, whole grains, olive oil, fish and nuts. Limits red meat and processed foods. Proven benefits: reduced risk of heart disease, diabetes and cancer.
glossary.t37def: Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension — a diet designed to lower blood pressure. Based on vegetables, fruits, low-fat dairy and whole grains. Limits sodium (<2300 mg/day), saturated fats and sugar. Clinically proven effectiveness for hypertension.
glossary.t38def: A nutritional strategy involving cyclical alternation between eating and fasting. Popular patterns: 16/8 (16h fast, 8h eating window), 5:2 (5 normal days, 2 days ~500 kcal). Potential benefits: improved insulin sensitivity, autophagy, weight loss. Not recommended for pregnant women, children or people with eating disorders.
